Idiosyncratic

/id-ee-uh-sin-KRAT-ik/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Idiosyncratic means peculiar to one particular person or thing; marked by highly individual quirks.

Idiosyncratic means peculiar to one particular person or thing; marked by highly individual quirks. Everyone in the office recognized Mr. Petrov's idiosyncratic filing system, which sorted invoices not by date or name but by the color of ink used to sign them.

Worked Example

Before every free throw, the veteran point guard performed her idiosyncratic ritual: three dribbles, a slow spin of the ball against her elbow, and a whispered word no teammate had ever deciphered. No coach taught it to her, and no one else in the league shoots that way.

The ritual belongs to this one player alone, a personal quirk that nobody else shares, which is what makes it idiosyncratic.

How Idiosyncratic Sits Among Its Neighbors

Antonyms

conventional

conventional: following accepted custom

generic

generic: having no individual character

How Strong Is It? — personal → idiosyncratic → bizarre

personal vs. idiosyncratic

personal vs. idiosyncratic: A personal touch simply reflects someone's taste, while an idiosyncratic habit is so specific to one person that it becomes their trademark.

bizarre vs. idiosyncratic

bizarre vs. idiosyncratic: An idiosyncratic habit is odd in a way that fits one individual, but a bizarre one is strange enough to startle anyone who sees it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — idio-

Prefix — idio-: one's own, private (Greek idios)

Root — syncrat

Root — syncrat: a blending together, from Greek syn-, 'together,' plus krasis, 'mixture'

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: adjective-forming ending

Put it together

Put it together: Idiosyncratic is Greek through and through: idios, 'one's own,' joins syn-, 'together,' and krasis, 'a blending.' An idiosyncrasy is literally your own private blend, the one-of-a-kind mixture of habits and tastes that nobody else shares, and idiosyncratic describes whatever carries that personal signature.

Use the root in a new word: idiolect

Use the root in a new word: idiolect: Linguists call the way one single speaker uses language an idiolect, that person's own private dialect, built on the same Greek root idio-, 'one's own,' that opens idiosyncratic.
